hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.ysm_m: With YSM installed, Hex Casting can read and edit player models. A model is made of $(thing)groups/$ and the $(thing)cubes/$ inside them: groups follow the bones, while cubes make up the visible shape. Usually, read a player's model, follow its child groups to the part you want, edit its properties, and write each change back up the tree before applying the whole model.$(br2)For Read, Apply, and Restore, the target player must be in range and in the same dimension. Scrolls, Slates, and other items carrying model data belong with their world save.

Give Read Player Model a target player. It pushes a list of the top-level groups in the player's selected model onto the $(thing)stack/$. Keep the whole list; Apply and Export need it later. The target must be in range, in the same dimension, and have a YSM model that can be read. If the model is not ready yet, try again in a moment. This Great Spell costs no Media.

Takes no inputs. Creates an empty group named “bone”. Use property index 8 to name it, 9 to give it cubes, and 10 to give it child groups. Add the new group to a group in your model before applying or exporting; it costs no Media.
Takes no inputs. Creates a default cube. Use property indexes 0 and 1 to set its origin and size, and 7 to set its face UVs; then add it to a group's cube list (property index 9). Costs no Media.

Arguments, in order: a group or cube, then a property index. The index must be a whole number from 0 to 13. The pattern returns that property's value. Check the tables below and choose a property available on that object. Costs no Media.

Cube property indexes (origin, size, and pivot use model pixels; rotations use degrees; scale is a factor; UV coordinates and sizes use texture pixels):$(br)$(li)0 Origin: vector$(br)$(li)1 Size: vector$(br)$(li)2 Pivot: vector$(br)$(li)3 Rotation: vector$(br)$(li)4 Scale: vector$(br)$(li)5 Inflate: number$(br)$(li)6 Visible: boolean$(br)$(li)7 UV: a list of six faces in north, south, east, west, up, down order; each face is [u, v, width, height, rotation, visible]. Rotation can be 0, 90, 180, or 270.

Group property indexes (pivot uses model pixels; rotation uses degrees; scale is a factor):$(br)$(li)2 Pivot: vector$(br)$(li)3 Rotation: vector$(br)$(li)4 Scale: vector$(br)$(li)6 Visible: boolean$(br)$(li)8 Name: string$(br)$(li)9 Cubes: list of cubes$(br)$(li)10 Children: list of groups$(br)$(li)11 Texture size: vector, top-level groups only, in [positive width, positive height, 0] form$(br)$(li)12 Part label and 13 Source label: strings that can only be read. Other indexes do not apply to groups.

Arguments, in order: a group or cube, a property index, then a value. Use the value type shown in the tables; lists must contain the matching kind of item. The pattern returns the edited group or cube. Properties that do not apply, and read-only indexes 12 and 13, cannot be set. To include the change in your model, put the result back in its list and write it back up to the top-level group. Costs no Media.

Example: add a cube to an existing bone. Follow child groups with index 10, using index 8 to check their names; read the bone's cube list with index 9. Create a cube, set its origin and size, add it to the list, and write the list back with index 9. If the bone has a parent, put the edited bone into that parent's child list with index 10. Continue up to the root, then replace that root in the original full list. Keep the parts you did not edit.

Apply and Export need the complete root-group list you got when reading one model. Do not remove untouched parts or combine roots from different models. Add new groups and cubes to the model you read before applying or exporting them.

Great Spell. Inputs, in order: the target player and that player's complete root-group list. Temporarily applies the model to the player. The default cost is one Charged Amethyst's worth of Media; the server can change it. The temporary change ends when you cast Restore, the player leaves the server, or the player changes models manually.

Input: the target player. Restores the model they had before the temporary change. Costs no Media. The target must be in range and in the same dimension; leaving the server also restores the previous model.

Great Spell. Input: the complete root-group list of one model. Exports a copy to the caster's client under exports/createmanaindustry/ysm/. This does not change a player's current model, and the caster must be connected to the game. The default cost is one Charged Amethyst's worth of Media; the server can change it.

hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.indus: The times move on, and so does technique. Knowing Hex Casting well enough by now, I joined its lore to the ways of machinery — and from that union came these industrial patterns, and an industrialized craft of Media. Magic was never mysterious; Hex Casting is merely a craft lost for too long. I am good with it, and upon it I will build my glory.

Read the $(thing)Iota/$ stored on an item resting on a $(item)Depot/$ or $(item)Placard/$ straight off the block, pushing it onto the $(thing)stack/$ — no need to pick the item up.$(br2)Consumes one $(thing)vector/$ — the position. Miscasts if the target is not a Depot or Placard, holds no item, or the item bears no Iota.

Light a $(item)Blaze Burner/$ or $(item)Allay Burner/$ from afar. Consumes a $(thing)vector/$ (the position) and a $(thing)number/$ (seconds of burn) to add exactly that much burn time.$(br2)Media is charged per second at the burner's own burn rate, making this exactly as economical as pouring in $(media)Liquid Media/$. Burners without a Blaze inside cannot be lit; invalid targets end in a $(thing)miscast/$.
hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.trick: The Tricksters keep spells in knots, a path as intricate as Hex Casting though far apart from it. If I can harness their $(thing)spells/$, my line will want for nothing.$(br2)These pages hold two bridging patterns: one reads a Trickster spell from your held item, the other casts it — so that Trickster magic enters the Hexcasting $(thing)stack/$, mine to command.

Read a $(thing)Trickster spell/$ from the spell item held in your other hand, pushing the whole $(thing)spell tree/$ onto the stack as a $(thing)Trick Iota/$.$(br2)Costs no Media — pure reading. If no spell-bearing item is held, it $(thing)miscasts/$ and the stack is untouched.

Pop a $(thing)Trick Iota/$ — a stored Trickster spell — and run it in the Trickster execution environment. An optional $(thing)list/$ supplies initial arguments.$(br2)Spells that finish in the same tick push their result back onto the $(thing)stack/$; longer ones continue across ticks in the background and return nothing; failed spells log an error and leave the stack alone. Media is drawn from the environment's own store — a $(item)Spell Construct/$ or the caster's carried supply.$(br2)Inside a $(thing)spell circle/$, execution instead draws Trickster Media from the $(item)slate knot/$ embedded in one of the circle's $(item)Slates/$: right-click a written slate with a knot to embed it, and again to retrieve it.$(br2)Slate knots give spell circles a dedicated Trickster Media pool, letting Hex Casting drive Trickster spells within.

A $(thing)Trick Iota/$ is a Hexcasting Iota carrying a complete $(thing)Trickster/$ spell — an entire $(thing)spell tree/$ — just like any other Iota: storable in $(item)Scrolls/$ and $(item)Slates/$, writable into casting items by a $(l:createmanaindustry/casting_item_production)$(thing)Deployer/$, able to travel the stack.$(br2)Its contents render through the $(thing)Inline/$ library, so spell trees show fully in Iota displays and the like. $(l:createmanaindustry/trickster_patterns#createmanaindustry:read_trick_from_item)$(thing)Unknotting/$ creates it and $(l:createmanaindustry/trickster_patterns#createmanaindustry:execute_trick)$(thing)Knot-Working Gambit/$ consumes it — the bridge between Trickster and Hex Casting.
hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.casti: Crafting $(thing)casting items/$ has always been tedious, and never without a hexer's hand in it — far too slow for my liking. So I built a $(thing)sequenced assembly line/$: a $(thing)Deployer/$, a $(thing)Spout/$, and a $(thing)Mechanical Press/$ in three steps, turning out items indistinguishable from handiwork.

$(bold)Step One: Scribe/$ — a $(thing)Deployer/$ aims at a fresh casting item on a $(thing)Depot/$ and copies a pattern from an $(item)Iota-bearing item/$ — a $(item)Scroll/$, $(item)Spellbook/$, $(item)Abacus/$, $(item)Slate/$, or $(item)Focus/$ — yielding an $(thing)incomplete/$ variant. Run it again to inscribe further Iota.$(br2)The held item is never consumed.

$(bold)Step Two: Fill/$ — a $(thing)Spout/$ pumps $(media)Liquid Media/$ into the piece. Capacity by tier:$(br)$(li)$(item)Cypher/$ — $(item)640 Amethyst Dust/$$(br)$(li)$(item)Trinket/$ — $(item)6,400 Amethyst Dust/$$(br)$(li)$(item)Artifact/$ — $(item)64,000 Amethyst Dust/$$(br2)Each pour adds up to a bucket; fill in passes. Capacities are configurable.

$(bold)Step Three: Press/$ — a $(thing)Mechanical Press/$ stamps the inscribed, filled piece into a finished item, carrying over every $(thing)Iota/$, $(thing)pattern/$, drop of Media, and $(item)dye/$ — a complete casting item, ready for spellwork.
hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.media: Wielding Media in its crystalline form is a wasteful business — the liquid Media stored within casting items suffers no such loss. In ages past, a hexer could barely draw Media out of amethyst without the aid of spellcraft; with today's machinery, it is simply pressed out.

$(media)Liquid Media/$ is a $(thing)Create fluid/$ — raw Hexcasting Media condensed into a form that flows through $(thing)Fluid Pipes/$. It glows with a soft pink light, easy to spot in tanks and basins.

$(thing)Heated Compaction/$ converts amethyst materials directly into $(media)Liquid Media/$:$(br)$(li)$(item)Amethyst Dust/$ — 25 mB$(br)$(li)$(item)Amethyst Shard/$ — 125 mB$(br)$(li)$(item)Charged Amethyst/$ — 250 mB$(br2)Compaction requires $(thing)heat/$; an ordinary $(item)Blaze Burner/$ suffices.

$(media)Liquid Media/$ can be worked further:$(br)$(li)$(thing)Heated Mixing/$ turns it into $(item)Liquid Mana/$ at a 1:1 ratio.$(br)$(li)In a $(item)Kinetic Atomizer/$, that Mana is $(thing)mixed/$ into a mist of $(media)Liquid Media/$ vapour.$(br)$(li)A $(item)Condenser/$ set in the mist gathers it back into usable $(media)Liquid Media/$, closing the loop.$(br2)Mana flows between liquid forms as readily as you please.

Converting amethyst into $(media)Liquid Media/$:$(br)$(li)1 $(item)Amethyst Dust/$ — 25 mB$(br)$(li)1 $(item)Amethyst Shard/$ — 125 mB$(br)$(li)1 $(item)Charged Amethyst/$ — 250 mB$(br2)Outputs scale with the server's $(thing)mediaPerBucket/$ and Hexcasting's own $(thing)Media numbers/$.

The $(item)Phials of Media/$ that hold liquid Media seem to be of a peculiar nature — they can only be made through the art of $(thing)Make Phial/$. That is a craft lost to time; to work it, I must hunt down $(item)Ancient Scrolls/$ left in some forgotten corner.

Modern machinery suffices: hand an $(item)Ancient Scroll/$ carved with the $(thing)Make Phial/$ pattern to a $(thing)Deployer/$ facing a $(item)Glass Bottle/$ on a $(thing)Depot/$, and you will have an $(thing)incomplete Media Phial/$.$(br2)The scroll must bear the right pattern, or the craft fails.

Fill the incomplete phial with $(media)Liquid Media/$ through a $(thing)Spout/$, then $(thing)press/$ it under a $(item)Mechanical Press/$ — the result is a finished $(item)Phial of Media/$ holding the equivalent of $(item)64,000 Amethyst Dust/$.$(br2)A phial's capacity equals the Media you pour in: you decide how much power it stores.

A finished $(item)Phial of Media/$ exchanges $(media)Liquid Media/$ directly with Create's $(thing)fluid network/$. Set the phial on a $(thing)Depot/$ above a $(item)Drain/$: the drain siphons it out for transport by $(thing)Fluid Pipes/$ or storage in tanks, while a $(thing)Spout/$ pumps Liquid Media back in.$(br2)Phials make ideal $(thing)Media buffers/$ in automated hexing: release when scarce, refill when plentiful.

One bucket of Liquid Media holds the equivalent of $(item)40 Amethyst Dust/$, and a full phial holds $(thing)64,000 Dust/$ — roughly $(thing)1,600 buckets/$.$(br2)Do the math, and your line can juggle plenty and dearth with ease.

$(media)Liquid Media/$ is the heart of the whole line: amethyst pressed into liquid, stored in $(item)Phials of Media/$, poured into $(item)casting items/$ for spellwork, and fed to $(item)burners/$ as fuel.$(br2)One fluid, threading through the $(l:createmanaindustry/casting_item_production)$(thing)Casting Item Line/$ and the $(l:createmanaindustry/industrial_patterns)$(thing)Industrial Patterns/$ alike — the seed of an industrial Media economy.
hexcasting.page.createmanaindustry.indus: Industrial patterns need not be drawn by hand alone — this mod registers $(thing)Stonecutting/$ recipes dynamically at startup, stamping any Hexcasting pattern save for Great Spells straight onto a $(item)Blank Slate/$. The recipes mirror the installed pattern registry exactly — addons' patterns included.

To use it:$(br)$(li)place a $(item)Blank Slate/$ in a $(thing)Stonecutter/$$(br)$(li)scroll the list — recipes are grouped by mod namespace$(br)$(li)pick a pattern to get a $(thing)pre-patterned Slate/$$(br2)It transcribes like any other Slate through standard $(thing)Pattern Transcription/$.
$(thing)Great Spells/$ cannot be cut — not even when I know their drawing.

So this is what they call $(thing)Enlightenment/$ — a wondrous, strange feeling. A $(thing)Great Work/$... now that is a fine design. And now I see what Slates are for... $(thing)Spell Circles/$? A fine thing indeed. Should the chance arise, I will set one among my newest machines — for I have seen enough. I will build the Great Work anew; I am destiny's own.

Take a census of a spell circle: it inspects the circle's own bounds — the region told of by $(thing)Lesser Fold Reflection/$ and $(thing)Greater Fold Reflection/$ — and pushes a $(thing)list/$ of the $(thing)entities/$ of every $(thing)player/$ standing within.$(br2)The dead are not counted, and order is not guaranteed. Cast outside a circle — via a $(thing)casting item/$, say — and it $(thing)miscasts/$.

A spell circle is itself a machine: a lattice of $(item)Slates/$ that, once activated, executes whatever pattern is inscribed upon it. And here it meets industry — a census of those who enter, ready to feed the $(l:createmanaindustry/casting_item_production)$(thing)production line/$.$(br2)Circle patterns are worked through the $(l:createmanaindustry/industrial_patterns)$(thing)Stonecutting/$ — stamp them on Slates and let the circle run.
